title: Rebasing a Feature Branch
description: Rebase a feature branch onto main, handle the workflow end-to-end, and understand when to rebase vs merge.

data.text: Rebasing a feature branch onto main keeps your branch up to date with the latest changes. It results in a linear history and avoids a merge commit at pull-request time. Mastering this workflow is essential for teams that value clean, reviewable history.

The standard workflow is: fetch the latest main, then rebase your feature branch onto it. This replays your commits on top of main's current tip. If your branch is already on the remote, push with --force-with-lease to update it.

data.title: Rebase a feature branch onto main
data.code:
# Step 1: Fetch the latest from the remote
git fetch origin

# Step 2: Switch to your feature branch
git switch feature/auth

# Step 3: Rebase onto origin/main
git rebase origin/main

# Step 4: If conflicts, resolve them, stage, then continue
git add src/auth/LoginService.cs
git rebase --continue

# Step 5: Push with lease (safe force push)
git push --force-with-lease origin feature/auth

data.title: Do not rebase a shared branch
data.text: Rebasing rewrites commit SHAs. If other developers are basing work on your branch, the rebase will cause their branches to diverge. Only rebase your own feature branches.

When a conflict occurs during rebase, Git pauses and marks the conflicting files. You resolve each conflict, stage the file, and run git rebase --continue. The rebase applies each of your commits in sequence, stopping at each conflict until you resolve it.

data.title: Rebase conflict resolution steps
items: Git stops at the conflicting commit and lists the conflicted files
Edit each file to resolve the conflict
Stage resolved files with git add
Run git rebase --continue to apply the next commit
Run git rebase --skip to drop the current commit entirely
Run git rebase --abort to cancel and return to the original state

data.title: Resolve and continue a conflicted rebase
data.code:
# 1. See conflicted files
git status

# 2. Edit the conflicted file(s)
# Remove conflict markers and keep the correct code

# 3. Stage the resolved files
git add src/auth/LoginService.cs

# 4. Continue the rebase
git rebase --continue

# Or abort if things are going badly
git rebase --abort

data.text: Rebase vs merge: the practical view

Merging main into a feature branch creates a merge commit. Replaying (rebasing) gives a linear history. For feature branches, rebasing is preferred because it results in a clean fast-forward merge. For integrating finished branches, a regular merge preserves the true integration timeline.

data.title: Rebase for updates, merge for integration
data.text: Use rebase when keeping a feature branch up to date with main. Use merge when you are bringing a finished branch into main. This hybrid approach gives you clean history without hiding integration events.

items.question: How often should I rebase my feature branch?
items.answer: Rebase at least once per day if main is active. Rebasing more often reduces conflict size and makes the eventual merge trivial.

items.question: Can I rebase a branch with multiple authors?
items.answer: Yes, but only if all co-authors agree. Rewriting commits that others are working on creates coordination overhead.

items.question: What if rebase takes too long?
items.answer: For very long branches, consider splitting the rebase: rebase onto an earlier main commit first, resolve conflicts incrementally, then rebase again onto the latest main.

items.question: Does rebase change the diff?
items.answer: No. The combined diff of all rebased commits is identical to the original. Only the commit IDs change.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Rebasing onto main keeps feature branches clean and up to date
Use git push --force-with-lease to safely update remote branches after rebasing
Resolve rebase conflicts incrementally; use --abort if things go wrong
Rebase for branch updates, merge for branch integration
Rebase frequently to keep conflicts small and manageable
